title: Overcoming the Modality Gap in Context-Aided Forecasting
one_liner: Adding descriptive context to time series only helps if the context is verifiably useful; this paper creates a massive dataset with verified context.
lead: Modern AI systems can see both numbers (a sales history) and text (a description of the market), but mixing them often makes things worse, not better, because the model wastes computational effort learning to ignore the unreliable text instead of focusing on the numbers. This paper figures out why: the text was never actually useful in the first place. By building a dataset where context is rigorously proven to help, the paper shows that when the text is real, multimodal models do win because the model now splits its focus across both signal sources equally.

problem.h2: The multimodal paradox: more information but worse predictions
paras: When you forecast (say, predict tomorrow's sales), you usually have two kinds of data: historical numbers (sales from past weeks) and descriptive context (notes about holidays, campaigns, or market news). Intuitively, a model that reads both should beat one that reads only the numbers.

But experiments show the opposite: models trained on text and numbers together often predict worse than models that ignore the text entirely. A naive attempt would be to just add more text to the training data and hope the model learns to use it—but that often fails because the text is not actually predictive. The real problem is hidden: the datasets used to train these models contain text that sounds useful but does not actually help the model predict better, because no one checked whether each description matched what the numbers were actually showing.

callout.html: When you add descriptive text to a forecasting model's training data, it often gets worse at predicting because the text was not rigorously chosen to actually be useful.

steps.text: Start with historical numerical data (sales, stock prices, traffic).
Create descriptions of what the numbers are doing ("Slight upward trend", "High volatility period").
Check that the description actually matches the numerical pattern, not random.
Assemble 7 million verified time-series windows with context proven useful.
Train a model that reads both numbers and text on this clean dataset.

object.h2: What the paper changes: the training dataset itself
paras: The paper does not change the model architecture or the training algorithm. Instead, it changes what the model learns from. Earlier datasets paired time series with context (text descriptions) that sounded relevant but were never checked. This paper creates a new dataset where every piece of context is rigorously verified to actually describe the temporal pattern.

hidden.name: context-to-time-series alignment
paras: Context usefulness is a measure of how well a text description actually explains what is happening in the numerical data. If a time series shows a sharp spike and the context says "quiet period", they are misaligned. If the context says "sudden shock", they are aligned.

This paper measures alignment by checking whether the description matches statistical properties of the numbers (trend direction, volatility level, pattern type). When alignment is high, the model can learn to trust the text. When alignment is low (which was the case in older datasets), the model ignores it.

heat.caption: Darker means higher alignment between text description and numerical pattern.

reads.html: Does the description match what the numbers are actually doing?
Statistical verification that context captures key properties of the time series.

mechanism.h2: Why verified context works: the model learns to trust it
paras: When a model trains on text that is genuinely useful, it learns to read both carefully. Here is the causal chain: (1) a description says the sales trend is upward; (2) the model compares this to the actual numbers and finds it is true; (3) the model assigns high weight to reading descriptions in future similar cases, because each success reinforces that paying attention to text improves predictions; (4) with enough verified examples, the model reliably uses context to forecast better because the pattern—text helps—has been repeated consistently.

Earlier datasets broke this chain at step 2: the descriptions were not carefully checked, so the model found many cases where text and numbers disagreed. The model learned that text was noise and stopped reading it, because mismatches train the model to expect predictions to fail when text is present. This paper re-enables the chain by ensuring step 2 always holds true—every description is verified to match the numbers before the model ever sees the pair.

stages.s: Raw time series with unverified context
Filter: does context match the numerical pattern?
Better forecasts using both modalities, because both text and numbers now point to the same truth

math.words: alignment score equals one minus the difference between the description's implied pattern and the actual numerical pattern
symbols: the trend or volatility implied by the description
the actual trend or volatility measured from the time series
the largest possible difference in the dataset

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Series 1: prices go up 5 percent. Description says 'modest gain'. |5 - 4| / 20 = 0.05. Alignment = 1 - 0.05 = 0.95 (high, this pair keeps).
Series 2: prices go up 5 percent. Description says 'flat period'. |5 - 0| / 20 = 0.25. Alignment = 1 - 0.25 = 0.75 (lower, but still kept if threshold is lenient).
Series 3: prices go up 5 percent. Description says 'sharp drop'. |5 - (-8)| / 20 = 0.65. Alignment = 1 - 0.65 = 0.35 (very low, filtered out).
The dataset keeps pairs with alignment >= threshold, so the model learns from only verified examples.

math.note: Higher alignment means the text accurately describes the numbers, so the model can trust it when forecasting, because the model learns that descriptions matching the data lead to correct predictions.

charts.title: Old method (unverified context)
charts.note: Text descriptions in older datasets did not actually help, so adding them made the model worse, because the model wasted learning capacity trying to decode contradictory signals instead of focusing on the reliable numerical data.

charts.title: This paper (verified context)
charts.note: When context is rigorously verified to match patterns, the model gains from reading it alongside numbers.

items.html: If the alignment verification is weak (threshold set too low), bad descriptions sneak into the dataset and the model learns bad habits again.
The paper generates context semi-synthetically to match patterns. If real-world context is written differently, the model may not transfer well.
Context that explains a trend but is hard to measure (e.g., 'market sentiment') will not pass verification and gets filtered out, even if a human would say it is relevant.
Verify context rigorously, use verified pairs for training, validate on real-world time series where ground truth is known.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a small forecasting task (e.g., predict next week's sales from past 8 weeks of data). Collect or generate pairs of time series and descriptions. Measure alignment for each pair using the formula above. Split the dataset into high-alignment pairs and low-alignment pairs. Train two models: one on high-alignment pairs, one on low-alignment pairs. Both see the same time series and text, but one was verified and one was not. Measure forecast accuracy on a held-out test set.
demo.closing: If verified context is truly useful, the high-alignment model should forecast better, because it trained on consistent signal rather than noise. If both models perform equally, alignment verification had no effect.
